originalTitle: Fines, indefinite motel stays and uncertainty: how a homeless camp exposed regional Australia’s housing crisis
summary: Rough sleepers at the Wilks Park encampment in Wagga Wagga were told to leave or be fined $1,100. As the social housing waitlist keeps growing, locals are stepping in to help as authorities flounder
content: Leigh Swansborough has just pulled into Wilks Park, one of the biggest homeless encampments in regional New South Wales. “You would think that people would be here today,” says Swansborough, an advocate for the people at Wilks Park. “But no one has shown up.” Tuesday was meant to be D-day for residents at the camp in Wagga Wagga. Compliance action requests – eviction notices by another name – had been given out by the council, asking those living there to move by 28 July or face a $1,100 fine. The encampment has been in the headlines since May, when a newborn baby died just 300 metres away on the riverbank after their mother gave birth in a tent. Almost three months later, the response to the growing crisis is fractured and confusing. The community is divided over how to manage the camp. Some, like Swansborough, have jumped in to help. Others side with the council: clear them out. This is the housing crisis in regional Australia. Once-affordable towns and regional centres have drawn in newcomers escaping the soaring house prices of the cities, in turn driving up local prices. Rents have soared, vacancy rates have plummeted, homelessness has grown and services are stretched to breaking point. Council reprieve and community help In Wagga Wagga, a small group of concerned citizens have stepped in to help – effectively acting as quasi social workers. They’re dropping off food, making sure people get to medical appointments, setting up meetings with Centrelink, visiting people in hospital, and one is even housing a resident. “We had hoped that there’d be a definitive moratorium on not moving people on,” Swansborough says. “But we still aren’t sure or positive that they would keep their word. So we all showed up.” Instead of a moratorium, the residents of Wilks Park who had been issued with a move-on notice were granted a brief reprieve. At a council meeting on Monday night, less than 12 hours before the residents were due to be kicked out, councillor Richard Foley successfully moved a motion to delay the evictions. So on Tuesday morning the handful of people left in the park were going about their business. Kim, an 82-year-old with dementia, was feeding the birds. Lincoln had started a fire for some to sit around. One young woman, in severe distress, was calling her mother, the police, an ambulance, anyone for help. Swanborough was with her, doing what she could. JJ was cooking up a meal with food dropped off from OzHarvest. She and her partner had lived in the camp for 14 months before they moved a week ago. “I packed up because I don’t want to have any problems,” she says. The 68-year-old has been homeless and living on the road for six years after rental prices in Sydney started going up beyond what she could cover with cleaning and kitchen work. They moved across regional NSW, eventually making Wilks Park home. Like many former residents, JJ moved out of the park to avoid the fine. She’s now parked at Narrandera, about 100km away, paying $300 a week to camp. At Wilks Park, JJ was known as the manager. You needed a cup of tea? A meal? Help late at night? To know the right person to call? She had it covered. “We’d call it JJ’s kitchen,” she joked. “Some people come from Canberra, some people come from Brisbane, for the cup of coffee – but it was only in my tent.” Between cutting up meat and putting out bread rolls, she explained that she comes back to help. She was the only resident from the camp to speak at the council meeting on Monday night – and not a single councillor asked her a question. Another woman, who told the meeting she was worried about parking on her street if a church developed their Sunday school, was asked seven. “I want to fight with the council,” JJ says. “Housing NSW, they say they’ve got a house for these people, but so far they’ve got nothing for them. They are all talk, no action.” Life at Wilks Park John, 38, is staying put, undeterred by the council’s repeated eviction notices. Because of his dog, 18-month-old YouWin, he can’t get into a motel. “I feel like I can stand my ground, or go into a motel, but if I do, what happens to little miss? She goes into a home or possibly gets put down,” he says. “She’s my support animal, therapy, the whole nine yards.” Asked what would help, John says flatly, “More homes.” But until they arrive, he’s stuck waiting on the social housing list, hoping not to be moved on. “They said they had something for everyone. I’m part of everyone. Indefinite [accommodation] for people with dogs? Yeah, great. But otherwise, don’t pull wool over people’s eyes.” A few tents down, Mark has set up his caravan. He is tall and articulate; between puffs of his rolled cigarette, he punches the air with jokes, winking when they land. Asked if he would go into a motel, he says he would prefer to “die on my feet with a smile on my dial, and be beholden to nobody”. “I don’t like to ask for help because I have in the past and been knocked back,” he says. His dog is walking around his legs, waiting patiently for him to kick a toy. She also wouldn’t be able to go into the motel. And Wilks is close to central Wagga, where Mark, who is on the disability support pension, can get to his medical appointments. “If it’s offered, that’s lovely, that’s wonderful. I’ve got the option of politely declining, which I’ve done. I don’t need assistance as long as I can get to my feet and get to that car.” ‘A desperate shortage of homes’ The expected wait time for social housing in Wagga is now between five and 10 years, and the town’s biggest social housing project – Tolland estate – won’t be completed until 2030. The number of dwellings went from 1,449 in 2021, to 1,310 in 2025, while priority waitlist applicants went from 17 in June 2021 to 102 in June 2025.
